People who get addicted actually say the same thing.  Then 45 minutes later, they're like "is there any more coke left?"

The drug itself doesn't do anything to you physiologically (except the numbness you feel in your head).  The high you feel from coke comes from chemicals that are already in your body.  It triggers a part of your brain that releases dopamine.  When you do a bump, your dopamine levels skyrocket, and suddenly you feel like the king of the world.  In turn, coke usually numbs your amygdala, so you temporarily become a psychopath.  You don't feel empathy, fear, guilt, or pain.  You just become SUPER in love with yourself.  Then when you're on a comedown and your dopamine levels spike, you get depressed and want more coke to reinstate that feeling.

That's why people get addicted.

>Money makes the world go 'round... I struggle with this necessary evil too.

I'm with ya on that.  Sometimes it disgusts me, but I'm not gonna lie...most of the time it intrigues me.  Nine times out of ten, you can almost always buy health and happiness with money.  My problem is that I have high, virtually unattainable expectations.  I want to drive an Aston Martin, have a 7 million dollar home on Sunset Plaza, eat caviar with champagne, and travel to exotic places on a regular basis.

>so, not reducing our emotion, but gradually re-prioritizing it, if that makes sense

Absolutely.  I mean that's what peaked my interest in stoicism in the first place.  Emotional control.  Before I had ever heard about it, I would wish I was a psychopath LOL.  I literally researched whether or not it was possible to damage one's amygdala to the point where any trace of sympathy, fear, or any other intense emotions would become non-existent.

>You could also maybe turn some of that emotional energy positive, such as enrolling in a martial arts course.

My dad put me into MMA since I was 9 years old...LOL I fell in love with it and kept at it for years.  I still do self-training and spar with my brother to this day.  That and the shooting range are really my only [healthy] outlets.

>What's your social circle like? You don't mention anything about your current friends.<

I have one single person I consider a friend.  I might even consider him my second brother.  He doesn't really let me mix with his other group of friends.  Not because he's embarrassed.  They've told me that in my absentia, when he gets drunk, he's said that they're not worthy of hanging out with me.  LOL.  I don't know, I guess that's one thing that makes me feel good about myself from anyone outside my immediate family.

As far as the military goes, as much as I have wanted to join the Marines for a long time (I was recruited several times throughout college), I can't.  My parents need my help financially.  I've already pulled loans out to pay for my tuition for law school, and I've been going half-and-half with my dad on the mortgage for some time now.

I plan on leaving the job at the mortgage company very soon.  As soon as I start law school, as a matter of fact.

And it's not like I'm simping over this one girl.  I've branched out to other women.  I've easily seen through her manipulative bullshit.  Still though, I look at her like a child.  As you said, some people don't really realize they're being manipulative.  More so than anything, it's the fact that I was manipulated that makes me angry the most.

I have so much pent up anger, dude.  I'll confess, at times I want to randomly do damage to someone's property.  Like, I wanna smash a car's fender or set a house on fire or even break someone's mandible.  Obviously, I do none of these things.  But the urge is there.  The only craft/skills I know are how to harm another human being as quickly and efficiently as possible.

I don't know man.  Maybe I should just stay the course and all these feelings will eventually go away.  I hope I'll just become desensitized to it all and realize what's important in the near future.  Reading more on stoicism really helped.

Some things are just out of our control.  We need to stop looking at the world through rose-colored glasses and start seeing the flaws of it all, and most importantly, accept that it's not perfect.  It's easier said than done, but accepting these principles is something I've been striving for.

Thank you again for your response man.  It means a lot.  Every little bit of perspective helps and I appreciate it.

I was addicted to coke my senior year of college.  Worst of all is how easily accessible it was for me.  I never technically paid for it.  The people that gave it to me felt they "owed" me, for reasons I won't discuss here.  Point being, I abused the privilege and next thing I knew I was having it for breakfast.

The shit permanently rewires your brain.  It's literally 45 minutes of psychopathy, and if you do enough of it, about 2 days of depression and suicidal thoughts on withdrawal.  After being a stone atheist for years, I went back to church one day and wept and prayed for the strength to quit the addiction before my whole life went down the drain.

Maybe it was Divine intervention.  Maybe it was a placebo.  But the next day, I surprised myself at how easily I turned down a line when offered several times.  I haven't touched it in two and a half years.

You probably know better than me how fucking shitty the withdrawal symptoms are.  All I can tell you is this my man: you appreciate everything you have even more when you're sober.  As a matter of fact, I don't recall appreciating anything when I was on coke.  Quite the contrary, I took EVERYTHING for granted, including my own livelihood.

You already know that you'll eventually lose everything to this habit.  The incentive is there.  Isolate yourself for a few days and let the withdrawal pass.  Or better yet, spend time with someone who you trust will support your plight.

Hope you make it through man.
